newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU banks want Euribor to replace IBORs after EMU.
newsitem.headline: EU banks want Euribor to replace IBORs after EMU.

text.p: The European banking industry is preparing the launch of a euro-denominated Interbank Offered Rate (Euribor) which it hopes will replace national IBOR rates by 1999, an industry source told Reuters on Thursday.
"We are now looking at the practicalities of setting up a European-wide Euribor," a Brussels-based source told Reuters.

Current national IBORs such as the London interbank offered rate (LIBOR) or Paris interbank offered rate (PIBOR) are crucial money market instruments, as they serve as benchmark rates for eurobonds, swaps, futures and other derivatives.
In theory, national IBORs could continue to exist after the advent of European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999, as all participating currencies will be proxies for the euro.
But financial institutions are pushing to get an IBOR rate for the whole euro-zone.
"There is significant pressure to have just one rate," the source said.

Banking industry federations, the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA), the International Securities Market Association (ISMA), the Federation of European Stock Exchanges, the International Paying Agents Association (IPAA) and other industry groups discussed the Euribor project at a meeting about capital market conventions under EMU with the European Monetary Institute (EMI) in Frankfurt on Wednesday.
The EMI, the forerunner to a European Central Bank, does not want to sponsor Euribor, the source said. "They consider it should be an industry-sponsored rate."
In some countries IBOR rates are sponsored by national banking associations, in others it is the central bank.
IBOR rates -- the price at which banks lend unsecured money to each other -- are fixed daily, using quotes from a selected group of financial institutions.
They usually cover the entire money market maturity range from one month to 12 months. Some also cover overnight and one-week rates.
The source said no decisions had yet been made regarding the technicalities of the Euribor.
"We are still at a very early stage," he said.

The project aims to have a Euribor sponsored by the banking industry and is likely to set up a panel of selected banks from every EMU country and international banks active in the EMU area to contribute quotes.
The aim is to have a full maturity range from one month to 12 months, with some doubt about whether shorter rates will be offered.

The industry needs to agree soon in order to remove doubts about which IBOR will serve as the benchmark for the trillions of dollars worth of derivatives contracts which currently take their legal reference from national IBORs.

In a discussion paper to financial market players, ISDA has set an end of July deadline for all national IBOR sponsors to make up their minds on the issue. ISDA said it needs a clear decision so that it can prepare revised definitions in their derivatives contracts.
Industry observers said that there was bound to be some wrangling about Euribor in the weeks ahead, not only between banks, but also between national derivatives markets.

Continental European derivatives bourses see the advent of a Euribor as an excellent lever to prise away business from London's International Financial Futures Exchange (Liffe), which is likely to continue working with LIBOR.
The U.K. government has not ruled out taking part in EMU from its planned 1999 start, but its statements suggest early entry is very unlikely.
The British Bankers' Association (BBA) last month proposed a euro LIBOR interest reference rate as a benchmark for displaced national currencies from January 1999.
French Marche a Terme International de France (Matif), for instance, is in talks with U.S. and Asian derivatives exchanges about launching a Matif Euribor futures contract.
